key_points.point: The document highlights the potential for AI to act as a powerful research assistant that accelerates information gathering and synthesis. By automating time-intensive tasks, AI allows researchers to focus on higher-level inquiry and iterative development of ideas. This aligns with the accelerationist goal of using AI to augment human capabilities and boost organizational efficiency. The author notes, however, that current systems are primarily tools for 'normal science' rather than revolutionary discovery.
key_points.verbatim: While these systems compile existing knowledge rather than generating novel insights, they speed up an important part of the research process by automating the time-intensive work of information gathering and initial synthesis.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section: 'In addition to repeated encounters with the unusual...'

key_points.point: The author envisions a future where AI tools are as flexible and expansive as the early World Wide Web, allowing individuals to assemble custom services and research environments. This democratization of digital tools is seen as a prerequisite for generating new ideas and moving beyond the 'inflexible' nature of current chatbot interfaces. From an accelerationist perspective, this shift toward open, modular AI development is essential for unlocking human creativity. The document acknowledges that we are currently in an early, 'AOL-like' phase of AI engagement.
key_points.verbatim: The flexibility and expansiveness of the Web â€” the fact that anyone could assemble sites and services from servers, collections, and data from around the world â€” made it a much better environment for the generation of new ideas.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section: 'We may very well look back on our first years...'

key_points.point: The document asserts that AI models are rapidly increasing in capability, noting that current models are roughly three times as able as they were a year ago on academic exams. This empirical observation supports the accelerationist belief in the predictable, rapid growth of AI intelligence. The author uses this to frame the current state of AI as a powerful, albeit currently limited, force for research. The caveat is that 'ability' on exams does not equate to the ability to formulate novel, open-ended research questions.
key_points.verbatim: The best LLMs had already surpassed me, and now, a year later, the latest models are roughly three times as able as they were a year ago on that same exam, still far from perfect but capable of producing accurate answers to very tough questions from the full range of academic disciplines.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section: 'A year ago, with tongue firmly in cheek...'

key_points.point: The document advocates for pairing AI's data processing power with human expertise to create interactive research environments. By using AI coding tools, scholars can build custom websites that allow for the exploration of latent connections across vast datasets. This approach champions AI as a 'super-assistant' that enables human-led discovery. The author emphasizes that this maintains the primacy of the human mind while leveraging AI's speed.
key_points.verbatim: The historian Benjamin Breen has used AI coding tools to rapidly build interactive environments that combine cultural heritage collections and LLMs so that he and other scholars can immerse themselves an era or set of documents in a free-form, thought-provoking way.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section: 'In addition to repeated encounters with the unusual...'

key_points.point: The document discusses the risk of AI-driven 'normal science' leading to a contraction in collective scientific reach, where AI tools automate established fields rather than exploring new ones. This reflects a concern about how AI adoption reshapes human cognitive and societal structures, potentially narrowing the focus of scientific progress. From a safetyist perspective, this highlights the need to understand how AI influences the trajectory of human knowledge and innovation. The author cites a study in Nature to support this observation.
key_points.verbatim: [The] adoption of AI in science presents what seems to be a paradox: an expansion of individual scientistsâ€™ impact but a contraction in collective scienceâ€™s reach, as AI-augmented work moves collectively towards areas richest in data.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section: 'The rapid acceleration, but overall normality...'

key_points.point: The author argues that AI systems are currently designed as 'answer-machines' that lack the situational awareness or curiosity to identify anomalies or ask pointed questions. This lack of self-understanding limits their utility in truly novel research. From a safetyist perspective, this reinforces the idea that current AI lacks the necessary 'situational awareness' to be a truly autonomous research partner. The document suggests that we must design systems that can highlight the unusual to prompt human minds, rather than just narrowing focus.
key_points.verbatim: AlphaFold is not going to pause one day, blank the screen of a startled biochemist, and ask pointed questions in a green phosphor font about the nature of proteins, which still have many strange and poorly understood functions.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section: 'The rapid acceleration, but overall normality...'

key_points.point: The document critiques the current interface design of AI, which prioritizes providing answers over facilitating inquiry. It suggests that to be more useful, AI should be designed to 'surprise' scholars or highlight what has not been studied, rather than just providing perfect alignment with user prompts. This aligns with the safetyist goal of ensuring AI systems are transparent and supportive of human oversight. The author notes that current LLMs are structurally biased toward summarization and narrowing.
key_points.verbatim: But it might be worth surprising scholars from time to time rather than always giving them perfect alignment. This surprise could take the form of a sidebar of items that wouldn't show up in a standard Boolean search.

key_points.point: The document emphasizes that human beings must maintain primacy in the research process, using AI as a tool for exploration rather than a replacement for human curiosity. It highlights the importance of human-AI collaboration where the human remains the driver of inquiry. This aligns with the safetyist focus on maintaining human control and oversight of autonomous systems. The author acknowledges that humans have many ways to conceive new ideas without technology, reinforcing the need for human-centric design.
key_points.verbatim: We should also remember that human beings still have plenty of ways to conceive new ideas that donâ€™t use AI, or any technology at all.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section: 'We may very well look back on our first years...'

key_points.point: The document argues that current AI models are structurally designed as 'answer-machines' that are poorly suited for the PhD-level work of formulating open-ended, uncommon questions. This design bias toward providing answers hinders the ability of AI to facilitate deep inquiry. From a skeptic perspective, this highlights the limitation of AI as a tool for genuine intellectual work. The author notes that while AI can reverse polarity to ask questions, it is fundamentally built to be on the 'A side' of Q&A.
key_points.verbatim: Structurally and interface-wise, Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini are mostly answer-machines for our questions right now. Yes, they can ask us questions in response to our prompts, reversing the polarity briefly, but they are designed to be on the A side of Q&A.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section: 'So the open-ended question I pose here is...'

key_points.point: The author frames AI-assisted research as 'normal science'—the important but incremental work of filling out existing models—rather than a revolutionary force. This aligns with the skeptic view of AI as a 'normal technology' that will be integrated into existing work practices rather than transforming them. The document argues that AI progress is impressive but ultimately bounded by the conceptual frameworks of a discipline. It explicitly distinguishes this from the idea of AI as a revolutionary force.
key_points.verbatim: In short, AI progress in some areas of research is impressive but nevertheless part of what the historian and philosopher of science Thomas Kuhn called â€œnormal science,â€  the important work of filling out existing models and answering lingering questions through careful experiments and studies.

key_points.point: The document advocates for focusing on how AI can be used to solve immediate, tangible research problems, such as identifying understudied areas or notifying researchers of new, relevant items. This reflects the skeptic intention to prioritize evidence-based, practical applications over speculative or sci-fi scenarios. The author suggests that we should design AI to 'surprise' scholars with unusual findings, which is a concrete, measurable improvement over current summarization-focused tools. This approach emphasizes the utility of AI as a tool for human researchers.
key_points.verbatim: Or a tool could scan all of the relevant material and return an assessment of what hasnâ€™t been studied in this particular area. This would be the opposite of AIâ€™s current inclination toward summarization and constant narrowing.

The author notes that while AI speeds up the research process, it does not replace the human mind's role in formulating new questions. This reinforces the idea that AI is a tool for 'normal science' rather than a source of creative breakthroughs.
